title: ⭐ Practice: the word, the dots and the doer

questions.prompt: A theatre website tells you to book your seats in advance. What does it ask you to do?

options.text: Bring something to read while you wait.
Insist that a place be given to you.
Keep a place for yourself before you arrive.
Write down everything you want in a notebook.

questions.explanation: to book is the verb English uses for keeping a place in advance, so the website is telling you to "Keep a place for yourself before you arrive." "Insist that a place be given to you." is what to demand means, and demand is the word a French speaker reaches for by mistake: asking politely and insisting are two different acts, and a theatre would be surprised by the second. "Bring something to read while you wait." and "Write down everything you want in a notebook." both answer the noun a book instead of the verb to book — the two words are spelt alike and have nothing else in common. Note that this verb can also stand with no object at all: be sure to book in advance.

questions.prompt: A welcome card is printed with some of its words unfinished, one dot for every missing letter. One line reads: "Our staff will be h.... to help you at any hour." The h is followed by four dots. Which word does the card ask for?

options.text: happy
helpful
here
honoured

questions.explanation: Four dots mean four letters after the h, so the word has five letters altogether, and "happy" is the only one of the four that has exactly five. All four would read perfectly well in the line — a welcome card could promise staff who are helpful, honoured or here — which is precisely why the meaning cannot settle it and the count must. "helpful" needs six letters after the h and "honoured" needs seven, so both overrun the dots; "here" needs only three and leaves one dot empty. Count the dots before you look for a word, and every candidate of the right meaning and the wrong length disappears at once.

questions.prompt: A pupil has copied out the Entertainment column of the module's table and one word has been put there by mistake. Which of these four belongs in the Science / Technology column instead?

options.text: amusement parks
contact lenses
hiking
opera

questions.explanation: Sort by asking what the word names, not what it took to make it. "contact lenses" name a piece of applied optics that people wear in order to see; nobody puts them on for an evening out, so they belong on the science and technology side. "opera" needs engineers to build its house and electricians to light it, and it is still an evening out, so the making of it does not move it. "amusement parks" and "hiking" name things people do with their free time, which is the whole definition of the entertainment column. The same question sorts the rest of the list: insulin, cloning, genes, laser, DNA, DVD and hard disc on one side; camping, canoeing, sightseeing and concerts on the other.

questions.prompt: A local paper reports that a lost wallet has come back to its owner. Which of these sentences keeps the passive right through and uses by only where it adds something the reader needs?

options.text: The wallet was handed in and was returned to its owner by somebody.
The wallet was handed in by a passer-by and returned it to its owner.
The wallet was handed in by somebody and was returned to its owner by the police.
The wallet was handed in by the school caretaker and was returned to its owner.

questions.explanation: Your grammar summary is exact: by is used only if a name or a noun giving necessary information is included. "The wallet was handed in by the school caretaker and was returned to its owner." names the caretaker, which is news, and then drops the doer of the second half, which is not. "The wallet was handed in and was returned to its owner by somebody." and "The wallet was handed in by somebody and was returned to its owner by the police." both hang a by somebody on a passive: the reader already knew a person was involved, so the phrase costs three words and tells him nothing. "The wallet was handed in by a passer-by and returned it to its owner." abandons the passive halfway and leaves the wallet doing the returning.

questions.prompt: A pupil has three reasons to give in her essay and must mark them so that a reader can count them. She has opened with To begin with. Which pair finishes the job?

options.text: For example, … Lastly,
Furthermore, … Lastly,
Secondly, … For instance,
To begin with, … Finally,

questions.explanation: A list of arguments has three slots — one phrase opens it, one adds to it, one closes it — and after To begin with the pair that fills the other two is "Furthermore, … Lastly,". "For example, … Lastly," puts an illustration where the second reason should stand: For example and For instance illustrate a point already made instead of adding a new one, so a reader counting arguments would count two and not three. "Secondly, … For instance," makes the opposite mistake and closes the list on an illustration. "To begin with, … Finally," opens the list a second time, and a paragraph cannot begin twice. The other set the module prints does the same three jobs: In the first place … Secondly … Finally.

questions.prompt: Sami wants to grant that online lessons cost him almost nothing and then object that they leave him alone all day. Which sentence makes both moves at once?

options.text: Although online lessons are cheap, and they leave me alone all day.
While online lessons are cheap, but they leave me alone all day.
While online lessons are cheap, they leave me alone all day.
While online lessons leave me alone all day, they are cheap.

questions.explanation: While opens the half that is granted, and the main clause carries the objection: "While online lessons are cheap, they leave me alone all day." grants the cheapness and objects to the loneliness, which is the order Sami wants. "While online lessons leave me alone all day, they are cheap." builds the sentence correctly and turns it round: it concedes the loneliness and ends by praising the price, so it argues for online lessons. "While online lessons are cheap, but they leave me alone all day." uses two connectors for one join, and English takes only one of the pair. "Although online lessons are cheap, and they leave me alone all day." adds an and that leaves the sentence with a subordinate half and no main clause to attach it to.
